title: Lemon curd
summary: A sharp, silky lemon curd thickened with egg yolks and finished with butter, sweetened with allulose so it stays smooth in the fridge.
steps: Whisk the zest, lemon juice, allulose, eggs, yolks and salt in a heavy saucepan (not aluminium, which reacts with the acid) until smooth.

Cook over low heat, stirring constantly with a spatula and scraping the bottom and corners, until it thickens enough to coat the spatula and reaches 77–80 °C (170–175 °F), about 6–10 minutes. Do not let it boil or the eggs will curdle.
Take it off the heat and stir in the butter a few cubes at a time until melted and glossy.
Press it through a fine sieve into a jar to remove the zest and any cooked egg.
Press plastic wrap onto the surface and refrigerate at least 2 hours; it thickens further as it chills. Keeps about 1 week refrigerated.
dairy_free_notes: With coconut oil the curd sets firmer when cold and has a slightly less creamy finish; let it stand 10 minutes at room temperature before spreading.
tips: Erythritol crystallises in a chilled curd; allulose stays smooth.
A double boiler makes the cooking slower but almost impossible to curdle.

origin.history: Fruit curds, also called 'lemon cheese', became popular in England in the 1800s as a spread for bread, scones and tarts. Earlier English recipes for creams and puddings made with lemon juice and eggs point the way, but the butter-enriched curd kept in jars is the nineteenth-century form. It remains a teatime staple in Britain.
